title: TA9-05227
frame:
Forum: Refugee Protection Division (first-instance tribunal).
Parties: the claimant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review: none; this is the first-instance decision.
How the layers nest here: The member of the tribunal is the author (layer 1). The claimant and the Minister make submissions to the member (layer 2). There is no earlier decision-maker unless the reasons describe a prior decision (layer 3). Testimony and documents are layer 5.

paragraphs.text: The claimant, XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX (age 56), is a male from El Salvador. He claims refugee protection pursuant to ss. 96 and 97(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act1 (IRPA).

The claimant states that he is a XXXX XXXX by profession. He says that he resided in XXXX, El Salvador and he had a XXXX and his own practice in XXXX XXXX XXXX. He states that the XXXX XXXX consisted of XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX and one XXXX XXXX.

He maintains that in late XXXX 2005, a man came to his XXXXX "XXXX" XXXX. He says that he XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX. The XXXX told the claimant that the XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX. The claimant states that while he was XXXX XXXX, XXXX XXXX ("XXXX"), who was a police officer and a XXXX XXXX of the claimant, came into the XXXX and was in the XXXX XXXX. When the XXXX left the XXXX XXXX also left a few minutes later. XXXX returned to the XXXX the next day and told the claimant that the XXXX was a wanted man and a member of the "La Mara 18" gang. XXXX said that he had XXXX XXXX just outside the XXXX.

The claimant alleges that after this incident he received numerous threatening telephone calls from the "La Mara 18" gang threatening to kill him and accusing him of "tipping off the police" regarding one of their members. He states that after he received the second telephone threat he went to the local police station in XXXX XXXX XXXX. He says the police tried to trace the calls but their system was unable to do so. He maintains they told him since they did not have proof that the calls happened they could not help him. He states that the next day he received a telephone call saying he should take care of himself since he took public transportation to work every day. He was very exposed to danger.

He alleges that in XXXX 2004, the XXXX in their complex received similar threats from "La Mara 18" and the same month he was shot and killed outside his home in XXXX XXXX by members of "La Mara 18". He states that the reason for the killing was unknown. He says that he became fearful and he went to the United States of America (USA) on XXXX, 2005, using a multiple visa he obtained in 1999.

He states that he could not afford a lawyer so he hired an immigration consultant who promised to help him obtain permanent residence in the USA. He says that the consultant told him that he would take care of everything and he should carry on with his life and even work. He maintains that on XXXX, 2006, US immigration officers picked him up and accused of overstaying his visa. He told them the consultant was looking after his immigration matters. They told him that there was nothing in their system and they arrested and detained him. He says his sister paid $5,000 US bail and he was released on condition that he appear in court on XXXX, 2007. When he appeared in court, the Judge granted him 120 days to leave the country voluntarily.
He arrived in Canada on June 27, 2007 and he made a claim for refugee protection on the same day.
I find that the claimant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection. ANALYSIS Identity
The claimant's oral testimony and the supporting documentation filed,2 establish his identity as a national of El Salvador. Credibility

In his Application for refugee protection3 the claimant stated that the persons who telephoned him said that they belonged to "La Mara 18". He also said that he was not sure why they threatened him. He also specifically stated that he did not call the police because "they would kill me more faster." In his original Personal Information Form4 (PIF) narrative he did not mention that he had gone to the police as a result of the telephone threats. In his amendment to the PIF, he stated that he went to the police after the second telephone call and they could not trace the call. He was asked why there was a difference between the statements in his application form, his original PIF narrative and his amended PIF. He could not offer an explanation but stated that his application form had been read back to him before he signed it but not after he signed it.

The claimant submitted a case5 from the Federal Court stating that in the absence of a verifiable record of what was said by the applicant at his interview, the Board should not use a Record of Examination to impugn the applicant's credibility because it was a breach of due process for the RPD to accept the Record of Examination as accurate in the face of the applicant's sworn statement in the PIF. However, in this case the statements were in the claimant's application and signed by him. He did not mention going to the police in his original PIF. If he had gone to the police it would have been an important fact to include in his application form or his original PIF. I conclude that he never went to the police on any occasion. Convention Refugee
The next issue is whether or not the claimant has a link to any of the five Convention grounds.

The claimant alleges that he fears members of "La Mara18" gang. The claimant submitted that because he was allegedly called a traitor that this could be considered an imputed political opinion. There is no persuasive evidence that the gang is so powerful or the corruption in El Salvador is so great that the gang could be considered intertwined with the government. There is documentary evidence that the government has actively initiated actions against the gangs in El Salvador.6 I conclude that, on a balance of probabilities, it could not be imputed that the claimant was expressing a political opinion against Mara 18.

There are a number of Federal Court cases, which have held that victims of crime, corruption7 or vendettas8 generally fail to establish a link between their fear of persecution and one of the Convention grounds in the definition of Convention refugee. The Board has been upheld in its finding of lack of nexus, where the claimant was a target of a personal vendetta9 or where the claimant was a victim of crime.10

The claimant's fear in this case is not linked to race, nationality, religion, real or imputed political opinion or to membership in a particular social group. There is no evidence that there was any link to any government organization. I conclude that the claimant is a target as a victim of crime or vendetta, and it does not provide the claimant with a link to a Convention ground. Therefore, the claimant is not a Convention refugee and the claim under section 96 of the IRPA fails. The balance of the analysis in this decision is pursuant to section 97 of the IRPA. Section 97 of the IRPA

The next issue is whether, on the balance of probabilities, the claimant is personally at risk to his life or at risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment or risk of torture, if he returns to El Salvador and the risk is not faced generally by other individuals in or from El Salvador.
I find that the claimant was not subjected to a danger of torture as there was no government involvement or complicity as required by the definition of torture.
I find that the risk faced by the claimant is one that is faced generally by all people in El Salvador and therefore he is not a person in need of protection.

Section 97(1) of the IRPA states: A person in need of protection is a person in Canada whose removal to their country or countries of nationality or, if they do not have a country of nationality, their country of former habitual residence, would subject them personally,... (b) to a risk to their life or to a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment if... (ii) the risk would be faced by the person in every part of that country and is not faced generally by other individuals in or from that country, (emphasis added)

A reading of this section of the IRPA leads to the conclusion that the risk, in addition to having to be personal also has to be one that would be faced in every part of the country and was not generally faced by others. There are therefore two separate concepts that have to be considered in dealing with this portion of the IRPA.

According to a sheet published by the Bureau for International Narcotics and Law Enforcement Affairs, youth gangs (maras) and a wave of violent crime that they have brought about are major threats to public security in El Salvador. It is reported that gang members are ultra violent and have built a parallel world with its own rules, initiation rites, economy and moral standards.11

The gangs engage in many illegal activities, from drug and arms trafficking to carjacking, grand larceny and trafficking in persons as well as witness tampering, rape, and murder. The MS-13 and its rival gang, the Mara 18 (MS-18) are the two most renowned maras in El Salvador, striking terror into the Salvadoran population.12

However, in accordance with the documentary evidence, the risk faced by the claimant from the MS-18 gang would be faced in every part of the country and is faced generally by all people in El Salvador. In addition, the criminal activity against him is faced generally by all individuals in El Salvador. As noted above, MS-13 and MS-18 strike terror in the entire Salvadoran population. In his testimony, the claimant also stated that when he was in El Salvador everyone was frightened of these gangs. The claimant here was one of their many such victims. The fact that the claimant may have been identified personally as a target because of suspicion that he gave information leading to the arrest of a gang member does not necessarily remove him from the generalized risk category, since the nature of the risk is one that is faced generally by others in the country. A generalized risk does not have to affect everyone in the same way. The Federal Court has upheld the Board in finding generalized risk for various victims of the gangs.13 14 15 The risk faced by the claimant would be faced by the claimant in every part of the country and is faced by all individuals in or from El Salvador.
Therefore, I find that, on a balance of probabilities, the claimant is not a person in need of protection. State Protection

I also considered the issue of state protection. I find that there is adequate state protection in El Salvador, and the claimant has not taken all reasonable steps in the circumstances of this case to pursue the available state protection. Moreover, the claimant failed to rebut the presumption of state protection, with clear and convincing evidence.

In assessing the issue of state protection, I am guided by a number of cases. The principles were applied to this case. There is a presumption, except in situations where the state is in a complete breakdown, that it is capable of protecting its citizens. A claimant who alleges that state protection is inadequate must persuade the Board that, on a balance of probabilities, the evidence establishes that the state protection is inadequate.16 A claimant can rebut the presumption by providing clear and convincing evidence of the state's inability to protect. For example, a claimant might advance testimony of similarly-situated individuals let down by the state protection arrangement or the claimant's testimony of past personal incidents in which state protection did not materialize. The onus is on the claimant to approach the state for protection in situations where state protection might be reasonably forthcoming.17 While the effectiveness of the protection is a relevant consideration,18 recent Federal Court decisions have held that the test for a finding of state protection is whether the protection is adequate, rather than the effectiveness per se.19 20 21 22 23 24 25 This was recognized in a Federal Court decision stating that "the preponderant case-law supports the test of an 'adequate' state protection rather than an 'effective or perfect' state protection."26 The protection need not be perfect.27 One accepted measure of assessment is whether the state is making "serious efforts" to protect its citizens.28 This standard continues to be applied in many Federal Court decisions.29 30 31 32

As stated above, no government is expected to guarantee perfect protection to all of its citizens at all times, and the fact that a state, in not always successful in protecting its citizens, is not enough to justify a claim, especially where a state is in effective control of its territory, has military, police and civil authorities in place and is making serious efforts to protect its citizens.33 Less than perfect protection is not a basis to determine that a state is either unwilling or unable to offer reasonable protection.34

Furthermore, the law states that the burden to prove an absence of state protection is directly proportional to the level of democracy of that state.35 The documentary evidence before the Board36 indicates that El Salvador is a constitutional, multiparty democracy. In March the voters selected Carlos Maurizio Funes Cartagena of the Farabundo Marti National Liberation Front (FMLN) as president for a five-year term in generally free and fair elections. Civilian authorities generally maintained effective control over the security forces.37

The National Civilian Police (PNC) is responsible for maintaining public security and the Ministry of Defense for maintaining national security. The military provided support for some PNC patrols in rural areas and gave support to law enforcement agencies for specific activities, including anti-narcotics and anti-gang efforts. The Ministry of Public Security headed the anti-gang task force. Approximately 5000 military personnel were deployed to join the police and anti-gang and other task forces, including an estimated 3000 additional soldiers deployed on November 6, 2009. Military personnel, however, do not have arrest authority. Through November, the PNC office of the Inspector General had received 2230 complaints of alleged police misconduct, referred 47 cases of these to special investigation units, and sanctioned 1181 officers in response to complaints filed during the year and prior years. These sanctions included 156 officers dismissed for misconduct and 762 suspended without pay for minor infractions. By year's end the Attorney General's office had prosecuted 462 police officers as a result of investigations begun during the year and in 2008. Insufficient government funding, lack of a uniform code of evidence, and isolated incidents of corruption and outright criminality interfered with the PNC's effectiveness. The PNC Inspector General reported that most PNC officers and police academy cadets received human rights awareness training during the year. There is nothing in the documentation before the Board to suggest that El Salvador is in a state of complete breakdown.

In this case, I find that the claimant did not go to the police on any occasion. If I am wrong in that finding, the claimant says that he contacted the police on two occasions. The original incident with the gang member occurred on XXXX, 2005. The claimant left the country on XXXX, 2005. This was only two weeks following the initial incident. This would not allow the police sufficient time to investigate the matter. In addition, claimant stated that he did not go back to the police to determine if their system was now able to trace any further telephone calls after they told him the system was unavailable after the second call.

I have considered the documentary evidence and submissions in regard to the general country conditions in El Salvador. It is acknowledged that El Salvador has one of the highest crime rates and murder rates in the world. It is also acknowledged that there is a large amount of gang activity El Salvador.

Documentary evidence38 states, The gang phenomenon presents a major challenge to Salvadoran law enforcement agencies, which have limited manpower, financial resources and technical capacity. However, the Salvadoran government does not have a policy or practice of refusing assistance to persons who receive threats or are otherwise victims of gang violence. Additionally, the US Embassy in San Salvador has no information to suggest that persons had been denied assistance from police authorities in relation to complaints they have made relating to gang violence or threats from gang members. Much of the government's current focus is on fostering and providing greater security for the public against gang violence. The Salvadoran government treats gang violence as a high priority, has expensed considerable sums to address the issue and has received technical assistance from the US and other countries to improve its law enforcement capabilities.

It is accepted that El Salvador has had difficulties with addressing criminality and corruption. The documentary evidence cited above indicates that El Salvador is making a concerted effort to deal with violence. This objective evidence suggests that although not perfect, there is adequate state protection in El Salvador, that El Salvador is making serious and genuine efforts to address the problem of criminality and police are both willing and able to protect such victims. The claimant has not established that were he to return to El Salvador today, protection would not be reasonably forthcoming or that it is an objectively unreasonable for him to seek protection.

The Board finds that the claimant did not take all reasonable steps in the circumstances of this case to pursue the available state protection. The claimant never approached the authorities in El Salvador for help or at most, he approached them on two occasions in a short period of time.
The claimant has failed to rebut the presumption of state protection with clear and convincing evidence.
Considering the evidence in its entirety, I find that the claimant has failed to rebut the presumption of state protection with clear and convincing evidence.

Having considered all of the evidence, I find that the claimant is not a Convention refugee or a person in need of protection. The Refugee Protection Division, therefore, rejects the claim for refugee protection.
